answer.sourceLine: This is Ephesians 4:32 in the King James Version (1611), word for word. It belongs to the letter that opens “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ” — though the exact English here is the KJV translators’ rendering of Paul’s Koine Greek, not his own words.

source.excerpt: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.
trail: The wording is a verbatim match for Ephesians 4:32 in the King James Version, confirmed letter for letter.
Bible Gateway’s KJV text gives the identical reading, including the archaic “be ye” and “hath forgiven you.”
The letter names its author in verse 1 — “Paul, an apostle” — though critical scholars are divided on whether Paul himself or a later follower wrote Ephesians.
source.excerptNote: Ephesians 4:32, KJV. The Greek word rendered “tenderhearted” is eúsplanchnoi — literally “of good bowels,” the seat of compassion in ancient thought.
source.rightsNote: The English wording is from the King James Version, first published in 1611 — long in the public domain in the United States. (In the United Kingdom the KJV remains under a perpetual Crown patent, but that does not affect US status.) Paul’s underlying Greek text has been public domain for nearly two millennia.

author.heading: About Paul the Apostle
author.metaLine: c. 5 – c. 64/67 AD · Apostle of Jesus Christ & missionary of the early church
author.bio: Paul of Tarsus was a first-century Jewish follower of Jesus whose letters to early Christian communities form a large part of the New Testament. The Epistle to the Ephesians, from which this line comes, opens in his name and is traditionally counted among his prison letters, though many modern scholars regard it as written by a later disciple in Paul’s tradition. Whoever held the pen, the exhortation to kindness, tenderheartedness, and mutual forgiveness became one of the most quoted lines of Christian ethics.

copyAttribution: "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you." —Ephesians 4:32, King James Version (1611)

misattribution.heading: Two honest footnotes
misattribution.intro: The attribution is essentially correct — this is a real verse from Paul’s letter — but two things are worth stating plainly.

items.why: Paul wrote in Koine Greek. The memorable English — “be ye kind… tenderhearted… hath forgiven you” — is the 1611 KJV rendering. Modern versions phrase it quite differently (“Be kind and compassionate to one another”).
The letter claims Paul, and tradition agrees, but a substantial share of critical scholars judge Ephesians to be “deutero-Pauline” — written in Paul’s name by a later disciple around AD 70–100.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Ephesians 4:32, in the King James English — a real line of the Pauline letters, correctly credited to Paul.

context.heading: Why it endured
lead: Ephesians 4:32 caps a passage urging believers to put away bitterness, anger, and malice. Its triple call — kindness, tenderheartedness, mutual forgiveness — grounds human forgiveness in the forgiveness the writer says God has already extended “for Christ’s sake.”
The King James phrasing gave the verse its lasting cadence in English, which is why it circulates on cards, samplers, and sermons in exactly this archaic form even as newer translations reword it.
